newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: RBNZ sees setbacks in its operating system.
newsitem.headline: RBNZ sees setbacks in its operating system.

text.p: The Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) said on Tuesday that while its operating system was very good at signalling the direction of movements in monetary conditions it believed necessary, it was not as good at signalling the desired magnitude of those movements.
In an article in its December quarter Bulletin, the RBNZ said one area in which it had come in for occasional criticism was the efficiency with which policy intentions were communicated.
"The Bank has for example never given a precise indication of how much adjustment in conditions is required in response to a statement.

"As a result, overshoots or misunderstandings sometimes occur, triggering a second statement in relatively quick succession (although these occasions have been relatively infrequent)," the article said.

In October, the RBNZ issued a statement saying a recent firming in monetary conditions had been greater than necessary. Just the week before, it warned markets after positive inflation data that conditions were easing too quickly.
The Bulletin article said that taking a medium to long-term horizon, the New Zealand system had worked "relatively well".

"The control framework has evolved as our understanding of how monetary policy and financial markets work has changed and grown. The system has proved capable of ensuring an effective degree of monetary control without relying on direct restrictions on the market activities of individual institutions or requiring the Bank to specify directly any particular interest or exchange rate," it said.

"The big moves in interest and exchange rates have occurred in a manner appropriate to our policy objectives, although from a short-term perspective desired 'fine-tuning' is sometimes difficult to achieve smoothly," the RBNZ said.

It said while it had not been as good at signalling the appropriate magnitude of movements in conditions, against that had to be set one of the key advantages of the current system, "that the Bank does not have to take concrete decisions to initiate all major changes in short-term interest rates".
